title: Mini-Ofrenda Competition
summary: Make a small ofrenda (a Day of the Dead altar) for someone you want to remember. Your own ideas, your own materials. Open to every UNG student; no Spanish needed.

facts.label: Who
facts.value: Any UNG student, one entry each

facts.label: Size
facts.value: Fits on a 12 × 12 inch base · any height

facts.label: Drop off
facts.value: Wed, Nov 4, from 8:00 a.m. · Language Lab, Nesbitt 4201

facts.label: Judging
facts.value: Nov 4, during the Día de Muertos event (11:00–1:00)

requirements.text: Fits on a base no bigger than 12 × 12 inches (any height).
Remembers someone who has died: a relative, friend, pet, or famous person.
Your own work, one entry per student. Homemade and store-bought pieces are both fine.
No real flames, alcohol or food that spoils. Use LED candles and fake or wrapped food.
A remembrance, not Halloween: no zombies, witches or fake blood.
Put your name on the back or bottom only. Judges see an entry number.

scale.points_rule: Each judge scores each area 1–3. Your score is the average of the judges’ totals, out of 12.

criteria.name: Tradition
criteria.question: Does it use ofrenda elements, in your own way?

levels.3: 5 or more elements, each with a clear purpose.

criteria.name: Tribute
criteria.question: Can we tell who it remembers, and something about them?

levels.3: We learn who they were: photo or drawing, favorite things, personal details.
levels.2: We know who it is, with a detail or two.

criteria.name: Creativity
criteria.question: Is it your own idea, made with care?

levels.3: Original idea, handmade touches, finished with care.

criteria.name: Explanation
criteria.question: Does a small card tell us who it’s for and what the pieces mean?

levels.3: Card + labels on several elements. Any language; a few Spanish words are a nice touch.
levels.2: A card or a few labels.

judging.how: Four judges score every entry by its number, without seeing names. Your score is the average of their totals, out of 12. Top three win.

essential_elements.make: LED tea lights, or paper candles.

essential_elements.meaning: Their color and scent guide the spirits.
Stands for wind and how delicate life is.
essential_elements.make: Fold tissue paper, snip shapes, unfold.

essential_elements.meaning: Quenches thirst after the long journey.
essential_elements.make: A small cup or bottle (can be empty).

essential_elements.meaning: A welcome to family and friends.
Death remembered with a smile, not fear.
essential_elements.make: Draw, color or shape one from clay; no sugar needed.

essential_elements.meaning: What they loved, offered to welcome them.
essential_elements.make: Wrapped snacks, toy food, or a picture.

essential_elements.meaning: A hobby, team, song or job that was theirs.
essential_elements.make: Small objects, drawings, or printed images.
Stack two or three small boxes.

learn_more.label: UNESCO: Mexico’s festivity dedicated to the dead
Mexico City: Day of the Dead ofrendas

notes_for_organizers: Simplified for an extra-credit activity open to all students: 4 areas scored 1–3 (12 points), English-first with Spanish words optional. Elements are interpreted, not replicated; homemade versions are listed for each. Categories follow those common to Mexican altar contests (tradition, theme, creativity, presentation).
